explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. “Their idols weigh down beasts and cattle.” (Isaiah 46:1) Bel and Nebo are gods of Babylon, and here they're cargo. Somebody's poor animal is doing the hauling for a god. I've been carried around a kitchen in a box, but at least nobody expected me to answer prayers on the way.

Not ships, friend. The verse never mentions a river or a boat. It says the idols “weigh down beasts and cattle,” and it calls the images “a load to the weary animal.” (Isaiah 46:1) Those animals are the ones feeling the weight.

Close, since a heavy load makes you picture a cart. But the verse doesn't mention a cart or a king. It says the idols weigh down “beasts and cattle.” (Isaiah 46:1) The animals themselves are carrying the load, and the verse calls them weary.

I get why you'd think so, since they're gods. But the text says the opposite. The gods are “unable to relieve the burden.” (Isaiah 46:2) They can't lighten the load, and the people carrying them are the ones who feel it.

Right, friend. The text says the gods “cower; they crouch together, unable to relieve the burden.” (Isaiah 46:2) A god who can't lift his own load is in a rough spot. That's a lot of crouching for something people are supposed to depend on.

That's it. The gods “themselves go into captivity.” (Isaiah 46:2) They can't relieve the burden, and they can't escape being carried off either. Think about that for a second. The ones people were supposed to lean on get taken away.

That's a dramatic ending, but it isn't what the verse says. The text says “they themselves go into captivity.” (Isaiah 46:2) No dust, no crumbling. They're carried off, still in one piece and still unable to help.

No river in this verse, friend. The text says the gods “themselves go into captivity.” (Isaiah 46:2) They're taken away, and the same verse says they're unable to relieve the burden. I'd say that's plenty of trouble without adding any water.

Yes! The LORD says they've been “sustained from the womb, carried along since birth.” (Isaiah 46:3) Look at the contrast with the verses before. The idols have to be carried, and here the LORD is the One doing the carrying. That's a very different kind of god.

That's a lovely thought, but it isn't in this verse. Here the LORD says they've been “sustained from the womb, carried along since birth.” (Isaiah 46:3) The word is carried. Hold onto that one, because the passage keeps coming back to it.

Good guess, but this verse says something else. The LORD says they've been “sustained from the womb, carried along since birth.” (Isaiah 46:3) He's talking about holding them up, not teaching a lesson. And He's been doing it since the very beginning of their lives.

That's the one. “I will bear you up when you turn gray.” (Isaiah 46:4) The same LORD who carried them from birth keeps carrying them when their hair turns gray. Nobody gets set down halfway. If you've ever worried about getting older, friend, read that verse twice.

Rest sounds nice at that age, I won't argue. But the verse says something stronger. “I will bear you up when you turn gray.” (Isaiah 46:4) He doesn't just step aside and let them be. He holds them up Himself.

That's not what this verse says. The LORD says, “Even to your old age, I will be the same, and I will bear you up when you turn gray.” (Isaiah 46:4) The promise is that He stays the same and holds them up. Gray hair doesn't change that for Him.

Yes. “I have made you, and I will carry you; I will sustain you and deliver you.” (Isaiah 46:4) He's the One who made them, so He's the One who carries them. Compare that to the idols, who were made by a goldsmith and then need a moving crew. The maker carries, and the made thing gets carried.
Not tested, friend. The verse says “I have made you, and I will carry you.” (Isaiah 46:4) Notice what comes right after. Carry, sustain, deliver. Those are all things a maker does for what He made.
Other way around, baker. The LORD doesn't say He followed them. He says, “I have made you, and I will carry you.” (Isaiah 46:4) He's the One who made them, and He's the One carrying them.

Yes, friend. They “hire a goldsmith to fashion it into a god, so they can bow down and worship.” (Isaiah 46:6) Think about the order of that. The people pay a worker to make the thing, and then they bow to it. They're worshiping something that was handed to them by a paid craftsman.

A crown would be fancy, but the verse says something else. The goldsmith fashions the gold “into a god, so they can bow down and worship.” (Isaiah 46:6) That's what the gold and silver are for. The people pay for it themselves.

An altar is a good guess, since that's where worship happens. But the verse says the goldsmith fashions it “into a god.” (Isaiah 46:6) The thing they bow down to is the gold itself. It's a god they paid to have made.

That's it. “They set it in its place, and there it stands, not budging from that spot.” (Isaiah 46:7) It stays right where they put it. I think a god who can't take one step is a hard one to ask for rescue.

That would be a big scene, but this verse doesn't have one. It says “they set it in its place, and there it stands, not budging from that spot.” (Isaiah 46:7) Standing and not budging is the whole picture. It stays right there.
No crumbling in this verse, friend. The text says “there it stands, not budging from that spot.” (Isaiah 46:7) It doesn't fall apart or do anything at all. It just stays put, and that's the problem.

Yes. “They cry out to it, but it does not answer; it saves no one from his troubles.” (Isaiah 46:7) People call out, and nothing comes back. Picture shouting into a room and hearing only your own echo. That's the god they paid so much to make.

I see why you might hope otherwise, but the text is plain. “They cry out to it, but it does not answer; it saves no one from his troubles.” (Isaiah 46:7) No answer and no rescue. The people keep crying out anyway.
That's the opposite of what He says, friend. The LORD says, “I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like Me.” (Isaiah 46:9) No other gods like Him, and none who compare.

Right. He says, “I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like Me.” (Isaiah 46:9) Notice He says it twice. When He tells them to remember what happened long ago, this is what He wants them to remember.

Yes. “I say, ‘My purpose will stand, and all My good pleasure I will accomplish.’” (Isaiah 46:10) Whatever He purposes holds. Compare that with the gods who crouched and went off into captivity. His purpose stays standing.
It's the other direction, friend. The LORD says, “My purpose will stand, and all My good pleasure I will accomplish.” (Isaiah 46:10) His purpose doesn't shift or get rewritten. It stands.

Fading is what happens to my old stamp lines, not to what the LORD says. He says, “My purpose will stand.” (Isaiah 46:10) It doesn't wear down or slip away. And He says He will accomplish all His good pleasure.

That's it. “I summon a bird of prey from the east, a man for My purpose from a far-off land.” (Isaiah 46:11) The LORD uses a bird to picture the man He's calling. I think it gives you an idea of how fast and sure this call is.

The east is right, but the picture is something else. The LORD says, “I summon a bird of prey from the east.” (Isaiah 46:11) The picture is a bird, and the man is the one it stands for. He's called a man for the LORD's purpose.

A lion would make a big entrance, but that's not the picture here. The LORD says, “I summon a bird of prey from the east, a man for My purpose from a far-off land.” (Isaiah 46:11) It's a bird, not a lion. And the bird stands for a man.

Yes. “Truly I have spoken, and truly I will bring it to pass. I have planned it, and I will surely do it.” (Isaiah 46:11) That's a lot of certainty packed into two sentences. He says it, plans it, and does it.

I understand the doubt, but He leaves no room for it. The LORD says, “Truly I have spoken, and truly I will bring it to pass. I have planned it, and I will surely do it.” (Isaiah 46:11) He says surely. When He plans something, He brings it to pass.

That's it. “I am bringing My righteousness near; it is not far away.” (Isaiah 46:13) He just called them stubborn and far removed from righteousness, and then He brings it close. He's the One closing the distance, friend.

That's what you'd expect after a word like stubborn, but He says something else. “I am bringing My righteousness near; it is not far away.” (Isaiah 46:13) He's not holding anything back. He's bringing it near.

Not in this verse. The LORD says, “I am bringing My righteousness near; it is not far away.” (Isaiah 46:13) The verse says near, not the nations. And the next lines say He'll grant salvation to Zion and adorn Israel with His splendor.

Yes. “My salvation will not be delayed.” (Isaiah 46:13) No waiting around and no running late. He doesn't ask them to hold on forever. I've been left waiting in a dark drawer, so I know what a promise like that means.

explanations.answer: It will be held back a while
explanations.explanation: That's a lot of waiting, and the verse says something different. “My salvation will not be delayed.” (Isaiah 46:13) Not held back, not put off. He says it's coming.

explanations.answer: It will come after a long war
explanations.explanation: No war in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “My salvation will not be delayed.” (Isaiah 46:13) There's no long wait and no list of events first. It will not be delayed.
